scope.start: 8b.13: the baraita of two people pulling a camel or driving a donkey (picks up mid-exchange on whether *rokhev* acquires)
scope.end: 10a.2: Ulla's reply that the pedestrian meant to acquire the find for himself from the outset (mid-exchange)

sections.title: Can *Rokhev* Acquire an Animal?
sections.gist: The Gemara continues to explore whether *rokhev* (sitting on an animal in riding position) acquires it, as *meshikhah* (pulling) and *hanhagah* (driving) do. Three baraitot seem to prove that it does: pulling and driving a camel or a donkey, a rider with another man holding the reins, and R. Eliezer on riding in the field. Each time the Gemara reads the rider as *manhig be'raglav* (driving the animal with his legs), so the question stays open.

children.title: First Tanna vs. R. Yehuda: Pulling a Camel and Driving a Donkey
children.gist: A baraita lets two people acquire an animal by pulling or driving it, while R. Yehuda allows each animal only the mode by which it is normally moved. The Gemara rejects the inference that riding doesn't acquire, and concludes that the first tanna rules out one unnatural mode, though which one is in doubt.

bullets.text: Baraita (first tanna): if two people were pulling a camel or driving a donkey, or one was pulling and one driving, they both acquire it “in that manner”. Pulling means leading the animal from in front; driving means urging it on from behind.
R. Yehuda: a camel is acquired only by *meshikhah* and a donkey only by *hanhagah*, since that is how each is normally moved.

The Gemara infers that since the baraita names only pulling and driving, *rokhev* does not acquire. It rejects this: riding acquires too, and the baraita names pulling and driving only to oppose R. Yehuda, teaching that even the reverse mode acquires.

Then the first tanna should have merged the cases: “two pulling or driving a camel or a donkey”. Since he kept the animals apart, he must agree with R. Yehuda about one reverse mode. Some say pulling a donkey fails, since a donkey won't move when pulled; others say driving a camel fails, since a camel isn't moved that way.
A *kinyan* must show the control an owner has over his property. Making an animal stagger forward in a way no owner moves it shows no such control, which is why the natural mode can matter.

children.title: What “In That Manner” Excludes
children.gist: In another version, the Gemara infers from the phrase “in that manner” that riding is excluded. It answers that the phrase excludes the reverse modes, and that the first tanna still differs from R. Yehuda on one of them.

bullets.text: In this version the challenge comes from the end of the first tanna's words: “they acquire it in that manner”. What does “in that manner” exclude? Surely *rokhev*.
No: it excludes the reverse modes, *hanhagah* of a camel and *meshikhah* of a donkey.

But that is exactly R. Yehuda's view. The Gemara answers that the two still differ on one reverse mode, which the first tanna allows: some say pulling a donkey fails for him, others say driving a camel. Either way the phrase says nothing about riding.

children.title: The Rider and the Man Holding the Reins
children.gist: A baraita gives the rider the donkey and the man holding the reins the reins. The Gemara again reads the rider as *manhig be'raglav*, and then has to explain why he gets none of the reins. Two emendations fall, Rav Ashi leaves the middle of the reins to no one, and R. Abbahu's defense of the baraita as written is refuted from a garment lying half on a pillar.

children.title: If the Rider Is Driving, Why Doesn't He Get the Reins?
children.gist: The Gemara reads the rider as driving the donkey with his legs, and emends the baraita so that each takes half the reins: the rider his half because the holder lifted it for him. But then the holder can't acquire his own half, since its far end is tied to a donkey he doesn't acquire.

bullets.text: Baraita: one man sits on a donkey and another holds its reins. The rider acquires the donkey and the holder the reins, which seems to prove that *rokhev* acquires.
The Gemara deflects: the rider is *manhig be'raglav*, urging the donkey forward with his legs, which acquires by everyone's account.

But if he drives the donkey and acquires it, he should acquire part of the reins tied to it as well. So the Gemara emends: the rider acquires the donkey and half the reins, and the holder the other half.

The rider's half is his because a *ben da'at* (a competent adult), the holder, lifted it for him. But how does the holder acquire his own half? The other end is tied to the donkey, which he doesn't acquire, so his *hagbahah* (lifting) never takes in the whole rein.
*Hagbahah* works by lifting the entire object off the ground. The holder raises only his end; the other end hangs from the donkey's head, held there by the animal and not by him.

children.title: The Holder Lifts the Reins for Himself, Not for the Rider
children.gist: A second emendation gives the rider nearly all the reins and the holder only the piece in his hand. The Gemara rejects it: lifting a find for another acquires for him only when one means to acquire it for him, and the holder means to acquire it for himself.

bullets.text: Second emendation: the rider acquires the donkey and almost all the reins, and the holder only the piece actually in his hand.
Rejected. Even granting *magbiah metziah la'chavero* (one who lifts a find for another acquires it for him), that works only when he lifts it meaning to acquire it for the other.
The holder lifts the reins to acquire them for himself. Since his *hagbahah* doesn't acquire them for him, it can't acquire them for the rider either.
The holder has no reason to act for the rider. His lift could have served the rider only as part of his own acquisition, and once that fails, nothing carries over.

children.title: Rav Ashi: The Middle of the Reins Belongs to No One
children.gist: Rav Ashi emends so that each acquires only what his own act reaches: the rider the donkey and the halter on its head, the holder the piece in his hand. The stretch of reins between them is acquired by neither.

bullets.text: Rav Ashi: the rider, who drives the donkey, acquires the donkey and the halter attached to its head; the holder acquires only what is in his hand; the rest of the reins, neither of them acquires.

The halter is part of the donkey, so it comes with the donkey and needs no one's lift. The holder's lift reaches only the piece he raised. The stretch between them was lifted by no one for anyone, so it stays free for anyone to take.

Why can't the rider's driving acquire the middle for him? Moving the donkey shifts the reins but doesn't lift them, and they are joined to the rider only through the animal, so his act never counts as *hagbahah* of them.

children.title: R. Abbahu: What One Can Pull Toward Himself Counts as Lifted
children.gist: R. Abbahu keeps the baraita as written: the holder acquires all the reins, since he could detach them and pull them to himself. The Gemara calls this an error, since it would give a garment lying half on the ground and half on a pillar to whoever lifted the ground half, and nothing to the one who lifted the half on the pillar.

bullets.text: R. Abbahu: leave the baraita as it is. The holder acquires the reins because he could detach them from the donkey and pull them to himself, so they count as his though he didn't lift them all.
Rashi reads this broadly: lifting part of an object, when one pull would bring the rest up as well, is as good as lifting the whole.

The Gemara calls R. Abbahu's statement an error. A garment lies half on the ground and half on a pillar; one person lifts the half on the ground and another the half on the pillar. By R. Abbahu, the first would acquire it all, since he could pull it off the pillar to himself, and the second nothing, which is certainly not the *halakha*.
Tosafot finds the refutation surprising: lifting the ground half when the rest is already raised sounds like a fair *hagbahah*, and R. Abbahu might accept that result.
With the baraita left unexplained, whether *rokhev* acquires remains unresolved.

children.title: R. Eliezer: Riding in the Field, Leading in the City
children.gist: R. Eliezer rules that riding acquires in the field and leading acquires in the city. The Gemara again reads the riding as *manhig be'raglav*, then asks why riding fails in the city. Rav Kahana says people don't ride there, Rav Ashi objects that an unusual act still acquires, and the Gemara sets the rule in a sale where the seller said “acquire it as people normally do”, then lists where riding in the city does acquire.

children.title: Riding and Leading as Two Kinds of *Hanhagah*
children.gist: R. Eliezer's baraita seems to prove that *rokhev* acquires. The Gemara deflects it by reading the rider as driving with his legs, and explains that the baraita lists him beside leading because it teaches two kinds of *hanhagah*.

bullets.text: Baraita (R. Eliezer): one who sits on an animal in the field, or leads it in the city, acquires it. This seems to prove that *rokhev* acquires.

Deflected: he is *manhig be'raglav*. Why list him beside leading, then? Because the baraita teaches two kinds of *hanhagah*, driving from the saddle and leading on foot, each in the place where it is normally done.

children.title: Does an Unusual Act Acquire? Rav Kahana vs. Rav Ashi
children.gist: Rav Kahana explains that riding fails in the city because people don't ride there. Rav Ashi objects from a purse lifted on Shabbat, which acquires though no one normally lifts it then. So the Gemara sets the baraita in a sale, where the seller told the buyer to acquire the animal as people normally do.

bullets.text: Why doesn't riding acquire in the city? Rav Kahana: people don't normally ride in the city, so riding there is not the way one takes hold of an animal.
The shiur cites Rashi that riding in town was avoided for propriety. Either way, an act out of place doesn't display ownership, even when it moves the animal.

Rav Ashi objects: then one who lifts a purse he found on Shabbat, which no one normally does because it is *muktzeh* (set aside from use on Shabbat), would not acquire it. Surely he does: what he did, he did. So riding in the city should acquire as well.

The Gemara answers that the baraita isn't about a find, which riding acquires even in the city. It speaks of a sale where the seller told the buyer to acquire it the way people normally acquire, so an unusual act falls outside what he allowed.
The seller's words set the terms of the transfer. With a find no one sets terms, so any act that takes hold of the object works.

children.title: When Riding in the City Does Acquire
children.gist: The Gemara lists the cases where *rokhev* acquires even in the city: in the public domain, where people do ride, and for an important person, a woman or a detestable person, for each of whom riding is the normal way.

bullets.text: If he rides the animal in the city's public domain, he acquires it, since people commonly ride there.
An important person acquires by riding even in an alleyway, since he always rides his animal rather than lead it.
A woman acquires by riding, since women don't normally lead animals; and a detestable person, who rides even where others don't, acquires by riding as well.
The shiur brings Rashi on the woman: she controls an animal better from its back. What counts is what is normal for this buyer in this place, not a fixed rule about cities.

sections.title: Pulling an Animal to Acquire the Vessels on It
sections.gist: R. Elazar asks whether *meshikhah* of an animal acquires the vessels loaded on it. Rava rules that it does not: even acquiring the animal along with them wouldn't, since a walking animal is a *chatzer mehalekhet* (a moving courtyard), unless it is bound. The Gemara then shows why a boat and a woman's basket are not moving courtyards: something else moves them.

children.title: The Seller Must Say “Acquire,” Not “In Order to Acquire”
children.gist: R. Elazar's question first needs rewording. A seller who says “pull this animal in order to acquire the vessels” hasn't told the buyer to acquire anything; the real question is where he says “pull this animal and acquire the vessels on it”.

bullets.text: R. Elazar asks: a seller tells a buyer, “Pull this animal in order to acquire the vessels on it.” Does the buyer acquire the vessels by pulling the animal?

The Gemara first fixes the wording. “In order to acquire” never tells him to acquire, and without that instruction he can't. The question must be where the seller said, “Pull this animal and acquire the vessels on it.”

Tosafot explains why the question isn't obvious. In *meshikhah* of an object, the buyer's own force moves it; here he tugs the animal, the animal walks under its own power, and the vessels move only because it carries them.

children.title: Rava: A Walking Animal Is a *Chatzer Mehalekhet*
children.gist: Rava rules that pulling the animal can't acquire the vessels, since even acquiring the animal with them wouldn't: an animal is a moving courtyard, and what can't acquire while walking can't acquire while standing either. The Gemara concludes that a bound animal does acquire what is on it.

bullets.text: Rava: it plainly doesn't work. Even if the seller said “acquire the animal and acquire the vessels”, the buyer wouldn't acquire the vessels.

Owning the animal could acquire the vessels only through *kinyan chatzer* (one's property acquiring what is placed in it). But a walking animal is a *chatzer mehalekhet*, and a moving courtyard does not acquire.
Nor does it help that the animal stands still while being pulled: whatever does not acquire while moving does not acquire while standing or sitting either.
The Gemara concludes that the vessels are acquired with the animal only when it is bound. Then it can't move on its own, and once he owns it, it serves as his courtyard.

A courtyard acquires as an extension of its owner's hand, which requires that it be firmly under his control. A living animal has a will of its own and can walk off, so even standing still it is not fully in his power; bound, it is.

children.title: Why a Boat and a Woman's Basket Are Not Moving Courtyards
children.gist: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua ask Rava about fish jumping into a sailing boat, and Ravina asks Rav Ashi about a *get* thrown into a walking woman's basket. Both answers are the same: the container itself sits still, moved by the water or carried by the woman, so it acquires.

bullets.text: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua ask Rava: fish jump into a boat as it sails. Is the boat a *chatzer mehalekhet*, so that its owner doesn't acquire them? Rava: no; the boat itself sits still, and it is the water that moves it.

Ravina asks Rav Ashi: a woman walks in the public domain, and her husband throws a *get* into her lap or into the basket on her head. Is the basket moving, so that she isn't divorced? Rav Ashi: no; the basket sits still, and she walks beneath it.

The disqualification applies only to what moves by its own will, an animal or a person. A boat carried by water or a basket carried by its owner has no will of its own, so it remains a valid courtyard for *kinyan chatzer*.

sections.title: Mishnah: The Rider Who Tells a Pedestrian “Give It to Me”
sections.gist: A rider sees a find and asks a pedestrian to hand it to him. If the pedestrian picks it up and says “I have acquired it,” it is his; if he says so only after handing it over, his claim is worthless and the rider keeps it.

bullets.text: Mishnah: one riding an animal sees a find and tells a pedestrian beside him, “Give it to me.” If the pedestrian picks it up and says “I have acquired it,” it is his: lifting it acquired it for him, though the rider saw it first.
If he says “I acquired it at the outset” only after handing it to the rider, he has said nothing, and the rider keeps it.
The Mishnah seems to imply that had the pedestrian lifted it for the rider, the rider would own it. Whether *magbiah metziah la'chavero* works is what the Gemara now takes up.

sections.title: Can One Who Lifts a Find Acquire It for Someone Else?
sections.gist: The Gemara brings R. Eliezer vs. the Rabbis on gleaning *pe'ah* for a named poor man. Ulla, citing R. Yehoshua ben Levi, limits the dispute to a rich man gleaning, which needs two steps of *miggo*; Rav Nachman holds they argue even when a poor man gleans, over *magbiah metziah la'chavero* itself, and tests both readings against our Mishnah.

sections.continues: Continues at 10a.3: the Gemara supports Ulla from the Mishnah's phrase “at the outset” in its last clause, and Rav Nachman explains the phrase otherwise.

children.title: R. Eliezer vs. the Rabbis: Gleaning *Pe'ah* for a Named Poor Man
children.gist: A Mishnah in Pe'ah has a man glean *pe'ah* and declare it for a certain poor man. R. Eliezer says he has acquired it for him; the Rabbis say he must give it to the first poor man he meets.

bullets.text: Mishnah (Pe'ah 4:9): one gleans *pe'ah* (the corner of the field left for the poor) and says, “This is for so-and-so, a poor man.”
R. Eliezer: he has acquired it for that poor man. The Rabbis: he has not, and he must give it to the first poor man he meets.
Rashi notes that the gleaner is not the field's owner, who may not take his own *pe'ah*; he is a third party.

children.title: Ulla: A Rich Man's Claim Needs Two Steps of *Miggo*
children.gist: Ulla, in the name of R. Yehoshua ben Levi, sets the dispute where a rich man gleans for a poor man. R. Eliezer reasons in two steps: he could become poor, and then could acquire it for another. The Rabbis accept only one such step, and all agree that a poor man acquires for a poor man.

bullets.text: Ulla in the name of R. Yehoshua ben Levi: the dispute is where a rich man, who may not take *pe'ah*, gleaned it for a poor man.

R. Eliezer reasons with two steps of *miggo* (“since”: what a person could do opens what he may do). Since he could renounce his property and become poor, the *pe'ah* is fit for him even now; and since he could acquire it for himself, he can acquire it for another.
The Rabbis: we say *miggo* once, not twice. The rich man's claim rests on one hypothetical built on another, so he can't acquire for the poor man.
Where a poor man gleans for another poor man, all agree he acquires it for him: since he could acquire it for himself, he can for another, a single *miggo*.

children.title: Rav Nachman: They Dispute Even a Poor Man Gleaning for Another
children.gist: Rav Nachman argues that R. Eliezer and the Rabbis dispute even a poor man gleaning for a poor man, so the question is whether lifting for another acquires at all. His proof is our Mishnah, which lets the pedestrian keep the find: on Ulla's reading it would fit neither view.

bullets.text: Rav Nachman to Ulla: say they dispute even a poor man gleaning for a poor man, so that the question is whether *magbiah metziah la'chavero* works at all.

His proof is our Mishnah. As to a find, everyone is like a poor man with *pe'ah*, free to take it. Yet the Mishnah lets the pedestrian, asked to hand the find to the rider, keep it by saying “I have acquired it.”

If the dispute includes poor for poor, the Mishnah follows the Rabbis: lifting for another doesn't acquire for him, so the find stays the lifter's. If all agree a poor man acquires for a poor man, the Mishnah fits neither the Rabbis nor R. Eliezer.

children.title: Ulla: The Pedestrian Meant It for Himself from the Start
children.gist: Ulla answers that the Mishnah's pedestrian says he meant to acquire the find for himself from the outset and never lifted it for the rider. So the Mishnah fits his view that lifting for another does acquire.

bullets.text: Ulla to Rav Nachman: the Mishnah speaks of a pedestrian who says, “I intended to acquire it for myself at the outset,” and never meant to acquire it for the rider.

So he isn't retracting an errand; he denies ever taking it on, and he is believed while the find is still in his hand. Had he lifted it for the rider, the rider would own it, since on this reading *magbiah metziah la'chavero* works.

returns_to.note: Returns to how the Mishnah's pedestrian keeps the find

key_terms.sense: sitting on an animal as an act of acquisition
key_terms.definition: Sitting on an animal in riding position, holding its reins, as a possible act of acquiring it. It differs from driving the animal forward, which acquires as a form of moving it.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Every baraita that seems to show that *rokhev* acquires is read as a rider driving with his legs, so the question stays open.

key_terms.definition: Acquiring a movable object, such as an animal, by pulling it or causing it to move toward oneself; the standard act of acquisition for movables. For an animal, it means leading it from in front.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Yehuda allows it only for a camel; R. Elazar asks whether *meshikhah* of an animal acquires the vessels it carries.

key_terms.definition: Acquiring an animal by driving it forward from behind, a form of *meshikhah* that causes the animal to move.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Yehuda allows it only for a donkey, and R. Eliezer's baraita is read as teaching two kinds of *hanhagah*: on foot and from the saddle.

key_terms.sense: a rider driving an animal with his legs
key_terms.definition: A rider who urges the animal forward by squeezing or kicking it with his legs, which acquires it as a form of driving.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Gemara uses it to deflect each proof that *rokhev* acquires, and then must explain why such a rider gets none of the reins.

key_terms.definition: Acquiring a movable object by lifting it off the ground; the object as a whole must be raised for the act to take effect.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The holder of the reins lifts only his end, and the Gemara asks how much of the reins that acquires, rejecting R. Abbahu's view that what one could pull over counts as lifted.

key_terms.sense: lifting a find on another's behalf
key_terms.definition: The question whether one who lifts an ownerless object meaning to acquire it for someone else thereby acquires it for him.
key_terms.on_this_daf: It explains why the holder can't acquire reins for the rider, and Ulla and Rav Nachman argue whether R. Eliezer and the Rabbis dispute it in the case of *pe'ah* and how our Mishnah fits.

key_terms.definition: A person's courtyard or other property acquires for him objects that come to rest in it, as an extension of his hand.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Acquiring the animal could acquire the vessels on it only through *kinyan chatzer*, which Rava rules out because the animal moves.

key_terms.definition: Property that moves, such as a walking animal, which cannot serve as a courtyard to acquire objects placed in it.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rava rules that a walking animal is one even when it stands still, unless bound, while a boat moved by water and a basket carried by a woman are not.

key_terms.definition: A line of reasoning that grants a person a power or a claim because he could have achieved the same result in another way open to him.
key_terms.on_this_daf: By Ulla, R. Eliezer lets a rich man acquire *pe'ah* for a poor man through two steps of *miggo*, while the Rabbis accept only one.

key_terms.sense: the corner of the field left for the poor
key_terms.definition: The portion of a field's crop left unharvested for the poor, which any poor person may take and the owner may not.
key_terms.on_this_daf: R. Eliezer and the Rabbis dispute whether one who gleans it for a named poor man acquires it for him, which the Gemara compares to lifting a find for another.

quiz.q: A man drives a camel from behind in order to acquire it. What does R. Yehuda rule?
options: He does not acquire it: a camel is acquired only by *meshikhah*, the way it is normally moved
He acquires it, since any act that moves the animal acquires
He acquires it only if he also rides it
He acquires half of it, since driving is the weaker mode
quiz.why: R. Yehuda allows each animal only its natural mode: *meshikhah* for a camel, *hanhagah* for a donkey.

quiz.q: One man rides a donkey, driving it with his legs, while another holds its reins. By Rav Ashi's reading, who acquires the stretch of reins between them?
options: Neither: the rider gets the donkey and its halter, the holder only what is in his hand
The rider, since the reins are tied to the donkey he acquired
The holder, since he could pull the reins to himself
They divide it between them
quiz.why: Each acquires only what his own act reaches; no one lifted the middle of the reins for anyone.

quiz.q: A garment lies half on the ground and half on a pillar; one person lifts the ground half and another the pillar half. Why does this case refute R. Abbahu?
options: His rule would give the whole garment to the first, since he could pull it to himself, which is certainly not the *halakha*
It shows that lifting half an object never acquires anything
It shows that the pillar acquires for the second person
It shows that whoever lifts first always acquires everything
quiz.why: R. Abbahu counts what one could pull over as lifted, which would leave the second lifter with nothing.

quiz.q: A seller tells a buyer to acquire an animal the way people normally do, and the buyer rides it in a city alleyway. Why doesn't he acquire it, though a found purse lifted on Shabbat is acquired?
options: In a sale the seller limited him to the normal way, and people don't normally ride in the city
Riding never acquires an animal
No act done in a city alleyway acquires
A purse can be lifted, while an animal must be pulled
quiz.why: With a find, what he did he did; in a sale, the seller's terms rule out an unusual act.

quiz.q: A seller says, “Acquire the donkey and acquire the vessels on it,” and the buyer acquires the walking donkey. Does he acquire the vessels?
options: No: a walking animal is a *chatzer mehalekhet*, which can't acquire; only a bound animal can
Yes, through *kinyan chatzer*, once he owns the donkey
Yes, but only at a moment when the donkey stands still
No, since vessels can be acquired only by *hagbahah*
quiz.why: What can move by its own will can't serve as a courtyard, even standing still; bound, it can.

quiz.q: Fish leap into a man's boat as it sails. Does he acquire them?
options: Yes: the boat sits still and the water moves it, so it is not a *chatzer mehalekhet*
No: a sailing boat is a *chatzer mehalekhet*
Only if he lifts them
Only if the boat is tied to the shore
quiz.why: Rava: only what moves itself is a moving courtyard; a boat is carried by the water.

quiz.q: A rider asks a pedestrian to hand him a find. The pedestrian hands it over and then says, “I acquired it for myself at the outset.” Who keeps it?
options: The rider: once the find is handed over, the claim is worthless
The pedestrian, since he lifted it
They divide it
It is set aside until the truth is known
quiz.why: The pedestrian is believed only while the find is still in his hand.

quiz.q: By Ulla's reading, a rich man gleans *pe'ah* for a named poor man. Why do the Rabbis say he doesn't acquire it for him?
options: His claim needs two steps of *miggo*, becoming poor and then acquiring for another, and only one is accepted
No one can ever acquire a find for another
The rich man must be the owner of the field
*Pe'ah* always goes to the first poor man to arrive
quiz.why: The Rabbis say *miggo* once, not twice; a poor man gleaning for a poor man needs only one, so all agree there.

judgment_calls: The three baraitot on *rokhev* (8b.13–9b.1) are children of one top-level section, since all serve the single question of whether riding acquires; each could have been top-level.
The two versions of the camel-and-donkey challenge (8b.13–9a.5 and 9a.6–9a.7) are sibling sections rather than one, since the alternative version reaches the same result by a different inference.

The first emendation and its objection (9a.9–9a.10) are kept in one section with the baraita, since the emendation exists only to answer the objection to the deflection; splitting it would leave a section without its point.
R. Abbahu's defense (9a.14–9a.15) is a sibling of the emendations rather than a separate top-level section: it answers the same difficulty in the same baraita.
The list of cases where riding in the city does acquire (9b.1) is a child of R. Eliezer's baraita, since it refines the sale ruling of 9a.19.
The Gemara's conclusion that a bound animal acquires (9b.6) stays within Rava's section rather than being its own, since it qualifies his rule.

The Mishnah (9b.9) is a top-level section of its own, and the *pe'ah* discussion a separate top-level section with a returns_to link from its last child, since the Gemara on the Mishnah works through an outside dispute before coming back to the Mishnah.
coverage_notes: The essay describes the first emendation as the rider's movement helping the man on the ground; the text says the rider acquires half because a competent person, the holder, lifted it for him, and then asks how the holder acquires his own half (9a.10). Followed the text.

The essay says R. Elazar's question on the vessels is never answered; the text has Rava rule that it plainly doesn't work, since even acquiring both the animal and the vessels wouldn't (9b.4). Followed the text.
The essay calls him Rav Abbahu; the text has R. Abbahu. Followed the text.
The essay presents the rule that what doesn't acquire moving doesn't acquire standing as the Gemara pressing Rava; in the text it is part of Rava's own statement (9b.5). Followed the text.
The segmentation titles the second emendation 'each gets distinct portion, middle remains ownerless'; in the text that is Rav Ashi's emendation (9a.13), as the essay itself has it. Followed the text.

The essay explains the city rule by Rashi's propriety; the Sefaria translation adds crowding as its own gloss. The outline gives the text's reason (people don't ride in the city) and keeps Rashi as a shiur point.
The essay calls the *zila* a lowly person with no standing to protect; the text says a detestable person who rides even where others don't. Followed the text.
The essay explains the woman by Rashi (better control from atop); the text says women don't normally lead animals. Both kept, the Rashi marked as shiur.
The essay's citation of the boat question ('Rav Pappa l'Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua l'Rava') is garbled; the text has Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua asking Rava. Followed the text.
The Gemara's support for Ulla from 'at the outset' (10a.3) and Rav Nachman's reply (10a.4) fall after this outline's scope.

daf_summary.summary: Discussion of: whether *rokhev* acquires an animal, tested on three baraitot (pulling vs. driving a camel or a donkey, the rider and the man holding the reins with its emendations and R. Abbahu's rejected rule, and R. Eliezer's riding in the field but not the city); R. Elazar's question on acquiring vessels by pulling the animal under them, which Rava rejects since a walking animal is a *chatzer mehalekhet*; and the Mishnah of the rider who asks for a find, with R. Eliezer vs. the Rabbis on gleaning *pe'ah* for another as Ulla and Rav Nachman read it.

takeaways.text: Whether *rokhev* acquires an animal remains open: each baraita that seems to prove it is read as *manhig be'raglav*, a rider driving the animal with his legs, which acquires as a form of moving it.

Lifting acquires only what was lifted. By Rav Ashi, the rider acquires the donkey and its halter, the holder the piece in his hand, and the reins between them no one; being able to pull the rest over does not count as lifting it.
An unusual act still acquires a find, as a purse lifted on Shabbat shows; it fails only in a sale whose seller required the normal way, which riding in a city alleyway is not.

A walking animal is a *chatzer mehalekhet* and can't acquire what is loaded on it, even standing still, unless it is bound. A boat moved by water and a basket carried by a woman are not moving courtyards.

A pedestrian who has not yet handed over a find keeps it by saying he acquired it; once he has handed it over, his claim is worthless. Whether he could have acquired it for the rider is the question of *magbiah metziah la'chavero*.

debates.question: Which way of moving a camel or a donkey acquires it?

sides.view: Both pulling and driving, except one reverse mode
Only the natural mode: pulling a camel, driving a donkey

debates.outcome: Which reverse mode the first tanna rules out is left in doubt.

debates.question: Does an unusual act of acquisition take effect?

sides.view: Riding in the city doesn't acquire, since people don't ride there
What he did, he did, as with a purse lifted on Shabbat

debates.outcome: An unusual act acquires a find; the baraita speaks of a sale where the seller required the normal way.

debates.question: Does one who gleans *pe'ah* for a named poor man acquire it for him?

sides.view: Yes, he acquires it for that poor man
No; he gives it to the first poor man he meets

debates.outcome: Ulla limits the dispute to a rich man and two steps of *miggo*; Rav Nachman extends it to a poor man, and the two argue over how our Mishnah fits.
